theme: Public-health and mobility indices: Google/Apple mobility archives, Cuebiq, SafeGraph/Advan/Dewey samples, Placer.ai-like foot traffic, mobility datasets by city

candidates.name: COVID19_mobility
candidates.what_it_holds: Aggregated, committed CSV/XLSX/ZIP mobility archive combining four sources: Google Community Mobility Reports (retail/recreation, grocery/pharmacy, parks, transit, workplaces, residential, country+sub-region+county level), Apple Mobility Trends (directions-request volume vs 13-Jan-2020 baseline, country/region/city), Waze driven-km percent change (country and some city level), and TomTom congestion rankings. Google span through 15-Oct-2022, Apple through 14-Apr-2022, Waze through mid-2022, TomTom continuing at time of archive. MIT license. Repo is archived/no longer updated (sources discontinued) but the historical CSVs remain committed.
candidates.why_useful: This is exactly the kind of consumer-mobility/travel-demand proxy series useful for reconstructing 2020-2022 travel disruption and recovery baselines relevant to STR/hotel demand cyclicality; also a ready single source for four different mobility indices instead of re-scraping each vendor. Google's own hosted CSV disappeared after the report shut down, so a committed mirror is the only easy way to get the full multi-year daily series now (fills a version of gap #5/#8 travel-demand context, pre-ABNB-scale IPO period baseline).
candidates.geography: Global, country + sub-national (US county, some cities) for Google; country/region/city for Apple; country + limited cities for Waze; city rankings for TomTom
candidates.size_hint: Multi-year daily panel across 4 sources, CSV/XLSX/ZIP, committed to repo

candidates.name: covid-19-open-data
candidates.what_it_holds: Google-maintained (now archived) open-data pipeline merging epidemiology, hospitalizations, vaccinations, and a dedicated Mobility table (Google Community Mobility metrics) across >20,000 locations at 4 aggregation levels (country/state/county/locality) as a daily time series through ~15-Sep-2022. Pipeline code (to re-run locally against sources) plus generated CSV outputs under CC BY; mobility subset still requires accepting Google's mobility-report ToS. Repo archived Nov 2024.
candidates.why_useful: Broader and better-structured than a raw Google Mobility CSV dump — includes county/locality-level granularity and is joinable to other macro/health covariates already in the same tables, useful for constructing a travel-demand recovery index by region (NA/EMEA/LatAm/APAC) for historical base-rate work.
candidates.size_hint: Large multi-table daily panel, generated CSVs (data volume not fully inspected)
candidates.license: Apache-2.0 (code); CC BY (generated data); mobility subset under Google ToS

candidates.name: google-covid-19-community-mobility-reports
candidates.what_it_holds: Rearc's automation/metadata wrapper distributing Google's COVID-19 Community Mobility Reports via AWS Data Exchange; repo itself has ~9 commits and does not commit the CSVs, just pipeline/metadata pointing at the AWS Data Exchange listing (external host).
candidates.why_useful: Confirms an auto-refreshing distribution channel existed (daily cadence claimed) but the actual bytes live on AWS Data Exchange, not GitHub, and the source report itself is discontinued — lower value than ActiveConclusion's committed CSVs.
candidates.time_coverage: Unclear / tied to defunct Google report
candidates.duplicate_of_holding: Same underlying Google mobility data as ActiveConclusion/COVID19_mobility, but without committed data

candidates.name: apple-maps-mobility-trends-covid-19
candidates.what_it_holds: Rearc's AWS Data Exchange distribution wrapper for Apple's COVID-19 Mobility Trends Reports (directions-request volume vs 13-Jan-2020 baseline, country/region + major metro city). No CSVs committed in-repo; ~9 commits, points to AWS Data Exchange listing.
candidates.why_useful: Same Apple mobility series as ActiveConclusion mirror; only useful if the AWS Data Exchange listing itself carries a longer/fresher series than the GitHub mirrors, which is unconfirmed.
candidates.duplicate_of_holding: Same underlying Apple mobility data as ActiveConclusion/COVID19_mobility

candidates.name: safegraph_py
candidates.what_it_holds: Official SafeGraph Python library for wrangling SafeGraph Places/Patterns foot-traffic data (joining, normalizing by population, home-panel-summary bias correction, POI category rollups). No data committed; requires a SafeGraph/Dewey data subscription or community-membership access to the underlying patterns files.
candidates.why_useful: If the team ever obtains SafeGraph/Advan/Dewey foot-traffic samples (e.g. via academic access), this is the standard toolkit to normalize POI-level visit counts into a usable travel/leisure foot-traffic index (hotels, tourist attractions, airports) as an ABNB demand proxy.
candidates.geography: US-centric POI categories (SafeGraph's core panel), extensible

candidates.name: SafeGraphR
candidates.what_it_holds: R equivalent of safegraph_py: functions for reading/aggregating SafeGraph Patterns and Places CSVs, distance calculations, and panel bias correction. No data committed.
candidates.why_useful: Alternative-language tooling for the same SafeGraph foot-traffic normalization task noted above; useful only if raw patterns data is separately obtained.

candidates.name: awesome-safegraph-datascience
candidates.what_it_holds: Curated list of SafeGraph-ecosystem notebooks, dashboards, and academic papers using foot-traffic data (retail, tourism, urban-park visitation, pharmacy demand). Points to SafeGraph's paid Data Bar marketplace and an academic/community free-access program (application-gated, not a public download) rather than any directly downloadable dataset.
candidates.why_useful: Useful map of who has built travel/leisure foot-traffic analyses on SafeGraph (e.g. urban park visitation, brand-level POI visit counts) that could be replicated if academic access to SafeGraph/Dewey Data is secured; not itself a data source.

candidates.name: SafeGraph-PublicCompanies
candidates.what_it_holds: Dewey Data's official notebook (SafeGraph-CompustatLinking.ipynb) matching SafeGraph Brand-level POI foot-traffic data to publicly traded tickers via SEC EDGAR + Compustat linking (ticker/fuzzy-name match). Requires a Dewey Data SafeGraph Brand subscription and WRDS Compustat access; no data or sample files committed.
candidates.why_useful: Direct evidence that SafeGraph/Dewey sell brand-level foot-traffic time series mappable to public tickers (which would in principle cover hotel/travel-adjacent public comps, though not Airbnb itself since it has no storefronts) — a method for a future workstream if paid Dewey access is obtained, not a free dataset today.
candidates.geography: US public companies with physical POIs

candidates.name: SafeGraph_Mobility_Workshop
candidates.what_it_holds: NYCDOT DEV Working Group workshop (Feb 2026) notebook + slide deck on SafeGraph mobility-flow analysis for NYC (net-flow maps, origin-destination matrices). No committed SafeGraph data, code/method only.
candidates.why_useful: Recent (2026) worked example of turning SafeGraph flows into an origin-destination travel index for a single city (NYC); a template if the team gets SafeGraph/Advan access for a market already in the Inside Airbnb panel.

candidates.name: google_covid_19_mobility_scrape
candidates.what_it_holds: Small scraper pulling Google's COVID-19 Community Mobility Reports website into structured data (2020, early pandemic). No large committed archive; low star count (4), minimal scope.
candidates.why_useful: Marginal — same underlying Google source as ActiveConclusion's larger, longer, already-committed mirror; only worth noting if the exact 2020 scrape logic is needed.
candidates.duplicate_of_holding: Google mobility data already better covered by ActiveConclusion/COVID19_mobility

candidates.name: db-safegraph
candidates.what_it_holds: NYC Mayor's Office of Data Analytics ETL pipeline for ingesting SafeGraph data into a city database (NYC Planning fork also exists: NYCPlanning/db-safegraph). Pipeline/infra code only, no committed foot-traffic CSVs (SafeGraph access is licensed to the city).
candidates.why_useful: Confirms municipal-government SafeGraph pipelines exist for NYC (a market already in the Inside Airbnb panel) but the underlying data itself is not public through these repos.

queries_run: gh search repos "google mobility reports data" --sort stars
gh search repos "apple mobility trends" --sort stars
gh search repos "COVID-19 community mobility reports" --sort stars
gh search repos "foot traffic dataset" --sort stars (empty)
gh search repos "COVID19_mobility archive" / "mobility data by city" --sort stars (empty)

WebFetch verification on: rearc-data google/apple mobility repos, ActiveConclusion/COVID19_mobility, SafeGraphInc/awesome-safegraph-datascience, Dewey-Data/SafeGraph-PublicCompanies, GoogleCloudPlatform/covid-19-open-data, ekinugurel/SafeGraph_Mobility_Workshop
notes: gh search repos hit its useful yield fast: exact-title queries for 'foot traffic dataset' and 'mobility data by city' returned zero results, and the API's free-text relevance ranking surfaces mostly toy student/COVID-era analysis notebooks rather than data mirrors, so 4 of the 6 allotted gh calls were spent confirming there was nothing further to find under those phrasings. WebSearch quota for the whole session (200/200) was already exhausted by other concurrent scouts before I could run a second round of web searches, so I relied entirely on gh search plus targeted WebFetch of individual repo pages (including one GitHub org, Dewey-Data, that markets itself as a SafeGraph data reseller) to verify contents; I could not cross-check Cuebiq, Advan, or Placer.ai-branded GitHub orgs by web search, and a `gh search repos` pass on those exact vendor names (Cuebiq/Advan/Placer.ai) was not attempted before the 6-call budget ran out — worth a follow-up scout with fresh gh quota. Best finding is ActiveConclusion/COVID19_mobility, a single MIT-licensed repo mirroring committed CSV/XLSX archives of Google+Apple+Waze+TomTom mobility indices 2020-2022 that are otherwise gone from their original hosts; everything SafeGraph/Dewey-related on GitHub is tooling/methods only, gated behind a paid or academic-application data access this scout could not verify as free.
